# Descriptive concept source excerpt

[Source paragraph 1; 2.2 Other Gas Laws; intervening text may be omitted]

Ideal gas behavior is approached when the distance between molecules (known as the mean free path) is large. Thus, molecules do not collide or interact with one another very

[Source paragraph 2; 2.2 Other Gas Laws; intervening text may be omitted]

$$
p \left(\mathrm {V} - m _ {\mathrm {g}} b\right) = m _ {\mathrm {g}} R T \tag {2.27}
$$

[Source paragraph 3; 2.2 Other Gas Laws; intervening text may be omitted]

where  $p$  is the pressure of the gas;  $V$  is the volume the gas occupies;  $m_{\mathrm{g}}$  is the mass of the gas;  $R$  is the specific gas constant;  $T$  is the absolute temperature; and  $b$  is the covolume of the gas.

[Source paragraph 4; 2.2 Other Gas Laws; intervening text may be omitted]

The covolume of the gas has been described as a parameter that takes into account the physical size of the molecules and any intermolecular forces created by their proximity to one another. Think of it as not having physical meaning but as simply a number that allows for a better fit to observed experimental data. The units of the covolume are cubic length per mass unit. Usually, the gas covolume is provided in the literature, but an estimation tool has been provided by Corner [7], which will not be repeated here since actual data exist.

[Source paragraph 5; 2.2 Other Gas Laws; intervening text may be omitted]

$$
p = \frac {\tilde {R} T}{\tilde {v} - b ^ {\prime}} - \frac {a ^ {\prime}}{\tilde {v} ^ {2}} \tag {2.28}
$$

items.quote:
# Descriptive concept source excerpt

[Source paragraph 1; 2.4 Thermodynamics; intervening text may be omitted]

Some of the concepts of thermodynamics were introduced in earlier sections, work and energy being the major ones. Here we shall look in detail at two ways of describing thermodynamic systems to proceed with our study.

[Source paragraph 2; 2.4 Thermodynamics; intervening text may be omitted]

We shall define energy for an arbitrary system as

[Source paragraph 3; 2.4 Thermodynamics; intervening text may be omitted]

$$
E = U + \frac {1}{2} m V ^ {2} + m g z \tag {2.38}
$$

[Source paragraph 4; 2.4 Thermodynamics; intervening text may be omitted]

We sometimes write Equation 2.38 in its intensive form as

[Source paragraph 5; 2.4 Thermodynamics; intervening text may be omitted]

Recall from our earlier discussions that an intensive property is the associated extensive property divided by mass.

[Source paragraph 6; 2.4 Thermodynamics; intervening text may be omitted]

For a fixed mass of material, undergoing some thermodynamic process, the first law of thermodynamics can be written as

[Source paragraph 7; 2.4 Thermodynamics; intervening text may be omitted]

The subscript 1-2 simply lets us know that the process began at some state 1 and ends at some state 2. The signs on the terms are very important. We assume a positive change in energy comes about by adding heat to the system and doing work on the system. Thus, work performed on the system is positive and heat added is positive. Different thermodynamics texts write the first law slightly differently, but if you understand that the net result of work on the system or heat transfer to the system is to increase its energy, then few mistakes will be made.

[Source paragraph 8; 2.4 Thermodynamics; intervening text may be omitted]

Caution is warranted at this point. Equation 2.40 does not say how the energy, once added to the system, is partitioned between potential (internal) energy and kinetic energy. This reveals something. Heat and work are added to or removed from the system at the system boundaries while the distribution of energy between internal or kinetic energy is done within the system.

[Source paragraph 9; 2.4 Thermodynamics; intervening text may be omitted]

We shall now explicitly write out Equation 2.40 for a Lagrangian system

[Source paragraph 10; 2.4 Thermodynamics; intervening text may be omitted]

Here we have neglected the gravitational potential energy terms and used the intensive form of the energy, multiplied by the system mass. As previously stated many times, we would like to use enthalpies instead of internal energies. If this is the case, we can rewrite Equation 2.41 using our relationship between the two from Equation 2.40. We shall use the intensive form of Equation 2.40 to yield

[Source paragraph 11; 2.4 Thermodynamics; intervening text may be omitted]

Here we note that  $h$  is the specific enthalpy and  $v$  is the specific volume.

[Source paragraph 12; 2.4 Thermodynamics; intervening text may be omitted]

We shall now examine the first law of thermodynamics in the Eulerian frame of reference. Recall that in the Eulerian frame, we chose a CV (real or imaginary) and observed how the energy within the volume changes based upon the energy carried into or out of it by any entering or exiting substance as well as any heat or work done at the system boundaries. It is convenient for us to write the first law in terms of the time rate of change of energy, heat, and work. We start by writing Equation 2.40 as a rate equation

items.quote:
# Descriptive concept source excerpt

[Source paragraph 1; 2.7 Fluid Mechanics; intervening text may be omitted]

Consider an arbitrary property  $N$  of a substance. We would like to see how this property is transported into and out of a CV. If we define an intensive property  $\eta$  such that

[Source paragraph 2; 2.7 Fluid Mechanics; intervening text may be omitted]

then we can write

[Source paragraph 3; 2.7 Fluid Mechanics; intervening text may be omitted]

$$
\frac {\mathrm {d} N}{\mathrm {d} t} = \frac {\partial}{\partial t} \int_ {\text {C V}} \eta \rho \mathrm {d V} + \int_ {\text {o u t f l o w a r e a}} \eta \rho \mathbf {V} \cdot \mathrm {d A} + \int_ {\text {i n f l o w a r e a}} \eta \rho \mathbf {V} \cdot \mathrm {d A} \tag {2.129}
$$

[Source paragraph 4; 2.7 Fluid Mechanics; intervening text may be omitted]

This equation defines how a property of interest is transported into and out of the CV. If we look at each of the terms, we see that this is an intuitively satisfying equation. The term on the LHS is the time rate of change (decrease) of any property of the CV over a time of interest. The first term on the RHS tells us how much of that property is stored in the CV over this time. The second term on the RHS tells us how much material has left the CV, while the third term tells us how much material has entered.

[Source paragraph 5; 2.7 Fluid Mechanics; intervening text may be omitted]

Now wait a minute! If we look at the signs on the second and third terms, they seem to be incorrect—should not the stuff leaving have a negative sign and the stuff entering have a positive sign? The answer to this is yes, but Equation 2.129 is written correctly. The key to this seemingly inconsistent sign convention lies in the fact that the dot product in the second term is positive when we define the area as a vector that points outward and is normal to the surface. Similarly, the inflow term will always lead to a negative number since the velocity vector points inward and the area vector points outward.

[Source paragraph 6; 2.7 Fluid Mechanics; intervening text may be omitted]

The ends of this cylindrical CV are designated as CSs. The inlet side is CS1 and the outlet side is CS2. If we would like to write an equation for how mass is transferred into or out of this CV, we set  $N$ , the flow variable in Equation 2.129, equal to  $m$ , the property of interest. When this is done, Equation 2.128 tells us that

[Source paragraph 7; 2.7 Fluid Mechanics; intervening text may be omitted]

We know mass can neither be created nor destroyed, so  $\mathrm{dm} / \mathrm{dt} = 0$ , then we arrive at what is commonly called the equation of conservation of mass, or the continuity equation. In a general form, it is given as

[Source paragraph 8; 2.7 Fluid Mechanics; intervening text may be omitted]

The first term on the LHS states how the mass in the CV is changing with time. The second term is the amount of mass exiting the CV, and the third term is the amount of mass entering the CV.

[Source paragraph 9; 2.7 Fluid Mechanics; intervening text may be omitted]

Simply put, this equation states that what comes into the CV equals what goes out of the CV.

[Source paragraph 10; 2.7 Fluid Mechanics; intervening text may be omitted]

When we apply this assumption to Equation 2.133 and note that  $\mathbf{V} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{A}$  is negative at CS1 (because the vectors have opposite directions) and positive at CS2, we obtain the following simple relationship:

[Source paragraph 11; 2.7 Fluid Mechanics; intervening text may be omitted]

Thus, under the steady flow assumption, the mass flow rate  $m$  is constant.

items.quote:
# Descriptive concept source excerpt

[Source paragraph 1; 3.2.3 运动微分方程与伯努利方程; intervening text may be omitted]

运动微分方程是牛顿第二运动定律在流体力学中的表达形式。在某些规定的条件下对运动微分方程积分就得到伯努利方程。

[Source paragraph 2; 3.2.3 运动微分方程与伯努利方程; intervening text may be omitted]

对理想流体，欧拉运动微分方程为：

[Source paragraph 3; 3.2.3 运动微分方程与伯努利方程; intervening text may be omitted]

$$
\frac {\partial \boldsymbol {v}}{\partial t} + (\boldsymbol {v} \cdot \nabla) \boldsymbol {v} = \boldsymbol {F} - \frac {1}{\rho} \nabla p \tag {3.7}
$$

[Source paragraph 4; 3.2.3 运动微分方程与伯努利方程; intervening text may be omitted]

如果流动满足：i 流动是定常的（各参量对时间的偏导数为零）；ii 质量力是有势力；iii 流体是正压性的（密度可以只表示为压力的函数）或不可压缩，则可以将欧拉运动微分方程沿着流线积分，得：

[Source paragraph 5; 3.2.3 运动微分方程与伯努利方程; intervening text may be omitted]

$$
U + \frac {v ^ {2}}{2} + P = C \tag {3.8}
$$

[Source paragraph 6; 3.2.3 运动微分方程与伯努利方程; intervening text may be omitted]

式中  $P$  ——定义的压力函数， $P = \int \frac{\mathrm{d}p}{\rho}$ 。

[Source paragraph 7; 3.2.3 运动微分方程与伯努利方程; intervening text may be omitted]

这就是著名的伯努利方程。方程中的三项依次为单位质量流体的重力势能、动能和压力势能。伯努利方程表明，当流动满足上述一系列条件时，在同一条流线上，重力势能、动能与压力势能之总和保持为常数。伯努利方程反映了理想流体流动中的机械能守恒。

[Source paragraph 8; 3.2.3 运动微分方程与伯努利方程; intervening text may be omitted]

实际流体由于存在黏性，在流动会有机械能向热能的转换。也就是说，在实际流体的流动中有机械能的损失，不符合式(3.9)。

[Source paragraph 9; 3.2.3 运动微分方程与伯努利方程; intervening text may be omitted]

对于有限过流截面的实际流体管流，将式(3.10)在管道截面上积分平均，即得到实际流体管流的伯努利方程：

[Source paragraph 10; 3.2.3 运动微分方程与伯努利方程; intervening text may be omitted]

需要指出的是，运用实际流体管流的伯努利方程时，截面应选在“缓变流”处，即流体在此处无折转，截面无突然变化。
